chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — _An apartment in the DUKE'S palace._
paragraphs: [Enter DUKE, ESCALUS, Lords and Attendants.]
DUKE. Escalus.
ESCALUS. My lord.

DUKE. To explain to you the principles of government would seem like me making a show of fine speeches, since I know that your own expertise in this exceeds anything my advice could add. So nothing remains but to trust your sufficiency to act as your worth allows, and let your judgment do its work. The character of our people, our city's institutions, and the standards of common justice — in all these you are as well versed as study and experience have ever made anyone we know. Here is your commission, from which we don't want you to stray. Call him here, I say — bid Angelo come before us. [Exit an Attendant.] What kind of stand-in for me do you think he will make? For you should know, we have with special care chosen him to take our place in our absence; we've lent him our authority, dressed him in our love, and given his deputation every instrument of our own power. What do you think of it?
ESCALUS. If anyone in Vienna deserves to receive such full grace and honour, it is Lord Angelo.
DUKE. Look where he comes.
[Enter ANGELO.]
ANGELO. Always obedient to your Grace's will, I come to learn your pleasure.

DUKE. Angelo, there is a certain quality in your life that to an observer fully reveals your history. Yourself and your gifts are not so much your own that you can waste yourself on your virtues, or they on you. Heaven treats us as we do torches — it does not light them for themselves; for if our virtues didn't go out from us, it would be all the same as if we had none. Spirits are not finely tuned except for fine purposes; nor does Nature ever lend the smallest particle of her excellence without, like a thrifty goddess, claiming for herself the glory of a creditor — both thanks and interest. But I am bending my speech to one who can already advertise my part in himself. So take this, Angelo: in our absence be fully ourself. Life and death, mercy and justice in Vienna live on your tongue and in your heart. Old Escalus, though first in rank for consultation, is your second. Take your commission.
ANGELO. Good my lord, let there be some further test of my mettle before so noble and great a figure is stamped upon it.

DUKE. No more avoiding it. We have with deliberate and prepared choice come to you; therefore take your honours. Our departure from here is so urgent that it presses itself ahead of matters of necessary importance. We shall write to you, as time and our affairs require, on how things go with us; and we will expect to learn what happens to you here. So, farewell. I leave the hopeful execution of your commission to you.
ANGELO. Still, give us leave, my lord, to accompany you part of the way.

DUKE. My haste won't permit it. Nor need you, on my honour, have any scruple about it. Your scope is as wide as my own — to enforce or to soften the laws as your soul thinks best. Give me your hand. I'll slip away privately. I love the people, but I don't like to put myself on display for their eyes. Though it works out well enough, I don't enjoy their loud applause and vehement cheers; nor do I think the man of sound discretion who craves it. Once more, farewell.
ANGELO. May the heavens give safety to your purposes!
ESCALUS. May they lead you forth and bring you back in happiness!
DUKE. I thank you. Farewell. [Exit.]
ESCALUS. I must ask you, sir, to give me leave to speak freely with you. It concerns me to look into the bottom of my office — a power I have, but of what strength and nature I am not yet instructed.
ANGELO. It is the same with me. Let us withdraw together, and we may soon have our satisfaction on that point.
ESCALUS. I'll attend upon your honour. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 1.

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — _A street._
paragraphs: [Enter LUCIO and two Gentlemen.]
LUCIO. If the duke, and the other dukes, don't reach an agreement with the King of Hungary, well then all the dukes will fall on the king.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Heaven grant us its peace — but not the King of Hungary's!
SECOND GENTLEMAN. Amen.
LUCIO. You conclude like that pious pirate who went to sea with the Ten Commandments, but scraped one off the tablet.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. 'Thou shalt not steal'?
LUCIO. Yes, that's the one he erased.

FIRST GENTLEMAN. Well, it was a commandment that would have stopped the captain and the rest of us from doing our job — we put to sea to steal. There's not one soldier among us who, when grace is said before meals, enjoys the petition that prays for peace.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. I never heard a soldier dislike it.
LUCIO. I believe you, because I doubt you've ever been anywhere grace was said.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. No? A dozen times at least.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. What, in verse?
LUCIO. In any measure, or in any language.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Or in any religion, I'd say.
LUCIO. Sure, why not? Grace is grace, regardless of any controversy — just as, for example, you yourself are a wicked villain, regardless of all grace.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Well, only a pair of shears could cut between us.
LUCIO. Granted; as there might be between the selvage and the velvet. You're the selvage.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. And you the velvet — fine velvet, three-pile no doubt. I'd as soon be the selvage of an English wool as be piled, as you are piled, for a French velvet. Do I speak with feeling now?

LUCIO. I think you do, and indeed with most painful feeling — feeling the pain of your own speech. By your own confession, I'll learn to drink to your health, but while I live, forget to drink after you.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. I think I've done myself in there, haven't I?
SECOND GENTLEMAN. Yes, you have — whether you're diseased or healthy.
LUCIO. Look, look, here comes Madam Mitigation! I've bought as many diseases under her roof as come to—
SECOND GENTLEMAN. To what, please?
LUCIO. Guess.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. To three thousand dollars a year.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Yes, and more.
LUCIO. A French crown more.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. You're always finding diseases in me, but you're entirely mistaken — I'm sound.
LUCIO. No, not sound as in healthy, but sound the way hollow things are sound. Your bones are hollow; immorality has feasted on you.
[Enter MISTRESS OVERDONE.]
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Hello there! Which of your hips has the worst sciatica?
MISTRESS OVERDONE. Well, well — there's one over there who's been arrested and carted off to prison who was worth five thousand of you all.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. Who's that, please?
MISTRESS OVERDONE. By Mary, sir, it's Claudio — Signior Claudio.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Claudio to prison? It can't be.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. No, I know it's so — I saw him arrested, saw him carried away; and what's more, within three days his head is to be chopped off.
LUCIO. But joking aside, I wouldn't want it so. Are you sure of this?
MISTRESS OVERDONE. I'm too sure of it — and it's for getting Madam Julietta with child.
LUCIO. Believe me, this could well be. He promised to meet me two hours ago, and he was always exact about keeping appointments.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. Besides, you know, this lines up pretty closely with what we were just talking about.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. And most of all, it agrees with the proclamation.
LUCIO. Come on! Let's go find out the truth of it.
[Exeunt Lucio and Gentlemen.]
MISTRESS OVERDONE. What with the war, what with the sweating sickness, what with the gallows, and what with poverty, my business has shrunk to nothing.
[Enter POMPEY.]
How now! What's the news with you?
POMPEY. That fellow over there is being carted to prison.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. Well, what has he done?
POMPEY. A woman.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. But what's his offence?
POMPEY. Groping for trout in someone else's private stream.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. What, is there a maid with child by him?
POMPEY. No, but there's a woman with a maid by him. You haven't heard about the proclamation, have you?
MISTRESS OVERDONE. What proclamation, man?
POMPEY. All the houses in the suburbs of Vienna are to be torn down.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. And what about the ones in the city?
POMPEY. Those are kept for seed. They'd have gone too, except a wise burgher put in a word for them.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. But all our houses of resort in the suburbs will be pulled down?
POMPEY. To the ground, mistress.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. Why, here's a change in the country indeed! What will become of me?

POMPEY. Come on, don't worry. Good counsellors never lack clients — even if you change your address, you don't need to change your trade. I'll still be your barman. Courage! People will have pity on you. You who have worn your eyes nearly out in the service — you'll be looked after.
MISTRESS OVERDONE. What's to be done here, Thomas barman? Let's clear out.
POMPEY. Here comes Signior Claudio, led by the provost to prison; and there's Madam Juliet. [Exeunt.]
[Enter PROVOST, CLAUDIO, JULIET, and Officers.]
CLAUDIO. Fellow, why are you parading me before the world like this? Take me to prison, where I've been committed.
PROVOST. I'm not doing it out of malice, but on Lord Angelo's special order.
CLAUDIO. So the demigod Authority can make us pay for our offence to the full weight of heaven's word — on whomever it will, it will; on whomever it won't, it won't; yet still it calls itself just.
[Re-enter LUCIO and two Gentlemen.]
LUCIO. Why, what's this, Claudio! Where does this confinement come from?

CLAUDIO. From too much liberty, my Lucio — liberty. As overeating is the father of much fasting, so every freedom, used immoderately, turns to restraint. Our natures pursue, like rats that gobble down their own poison, a thirsty evil; and when we drink, we die.

LUCIO. If I could speak so wisely under arrest, I'd send for certain of my creditors. And yet, to tell the truth, I'd rather have the foolishness of freedom than the morality of imprisonment. What's your offence, Claudio?
CLAUDIO. Anything I said would offend all over again.
LUCIO. What, is it murder?
CLAUDIO. No.
LUCIO. Lechery?
CLAUDIO. Call it that.
PROVOST. Come along, sir! You must go.
CLAUDIO. One word, good friend. Lucio, a word with you.
LUCIO. A hundred, if they'll do you any good. Is lechery being prosecuted that hard?

CLAUDIO. Here's how it stands with me: by a true contract I took possession of Julietta's bed. You know the lady — she is in effect my wife, except that we lack the formal public declaration. We held off on that only for the sake of a dowry still in the keeping of her friends, from whom we thought it best to hide our love until time had brought them round. But it happens that the stealth of our shared intimacy is now written on Juliet in characters too plain to hide.
LUCIO. With child, perhaps?

CLAUDIO. Unhappily, just so. And the new Deputy now standing in for the Duke — whether it's the fault and the dazzle of newness, or whether the body politic is a horse the governor rides, and he, newly in the saddle, lets it feel the spur straight away so it will know he can command; whether the tyranny lies in the office, or in the eminence that fills it — I can't quite say. But this new governor wakes up all the registered penalties which have, like unscoured armour, hung by the wall so long that nineteen years have gone by and none of them been worn; and, just for a reputation, he now slaps the drowsy and neglected statute freshly onto me. It's surely just for a name.
LUCIO. I'd swear it is. And your head sits so loose on your shoulders that a milkmaid, if she's in love, might sigh it off. Send after the duke and appeal to him.

CLAUDIO. I have done that, but he can't be found. I beg you, Lucio, do me this kind service: today my sister is to enter the convent and there receive her admission. Inform her of the danger I'm in. Plead with her, in my voice, to make friends with the strict deputy — tell her to approach him herself. I have great hope in that; for in her youth there is an unspoken, eloquent quality that moves men. Besides, she has a real gift when she chooses to use reason and discourse, and she can persuade.

LUCIO. I pray she may — both for the sake of others in your position, who would otherwise stand under heavy penalty, and for the saving of your life, which I'd be sorry to see foolishly thrown away at a game of tick-tack. I'll go to her.
CLAUDIO. Thank you, good friend Lucio.
LUCIO. Within two hours.
CLAUDIO. Come, officer, away!
[Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 2.

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — _A monastery._
paragraphs: [Enter DUKE and FRIAR THOMAS.]

DUKE. No, holy father — put that thought aside. Don't believe that the trifling dart of love can pierce a fully armoured heart. My reason for asking you to give me secret refuge has a purpose more grave and weighty than the aims and ends of burning youth.
FRIAR THOMAS. May your Grace speak of it?

DUKE. My holy sir, none knows better than you how I have always loved a retired life, and held it of little worth to haunt assemblies where youth, expense, and witless show prevail. I have handed over to Lord Angelo — a man of strictness and firm self-restraint — my absolute power and place here in Vienna; and he supposes I have travelled to Poland, for so I have spread the report through common ears, and so it is received. Now, pious sir, you will want to ask why I do this?
FRIAR THOMAS. Gladly, my lord.

DUKE. We have strict statutes and most biting laws — the necessary bits and bridles for headstrong weeds — which we have let slip for these fourteen years; like an overgrown lion in a cave that no longer goes out to prey. Now, like indulgent fathers who tie up the threatening birch only to display it in their children's sight for fear, not for use, in time the rod becomes more mocked than feared. So with our decrees: dead to enforcement, they are dead in themselves; liberty pulls justice by the nose; the baby beats the nurse, and all decorum is turned upside down.
FRIAR THOMAS. It was within your Grace's power to unloose this bound-up justice whenever you pleased; and in you it would have seemed more fearsome than in Lord Angelo.

DUKE. I fear, too fearsome. Since it was my fault to give the people so much room, it would be my tyranny now to strike and chastise them for doing what I allowed. For we authorize an act when evil deeds have free passage and no punishment. Therefore, indeed, my father, I have placed the office on Angelo, who may, behind the cover of my name, strike home — and yet my own nature is never present in the fight, never exposed to slander. And to observe how he governs, I will, as if a brother of your order, visit both prince and people. Therefore, I beg you, give me the habit, and instruct me how I may bear myself in person like a true friar. More reasons for this I'll give you at greater leisure; only this one for now: Lord Angelo is precise, stands on guard against envy, scarcely admits his blood flows, or that his appetite would prefer bread to stone. So we shall see — if power changes purpose — what those who only seem to be virtuous really are. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 3.

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — _A nunnery._
paragraphs: [Enter ISABELLA and FRANCISCA.]
ISABELLA. And do you nuns have no further privileges?
FRANCISCA. Aren't these large enough?
ISABELLA. Yes, truly — I'm not speaking as if I wanted more, but rather wishing a stricter restraint upon the sisterhood, the votaries of Saint Clare.
LUCIO [within]. Ho! Peace be in this place!
ISABELLA. Who's that calling?

FRANCISCA. It is a man's voice. Gentle Isabella, you turn the key and find out his business yourself. You may — I may not. You are not yet sworn in. Once you've taken your vows, you must not speak with men except in the prioress's presence; and then, if you speak, you must not show your face, or if you show your face, you must not speak. He's calling again. Please, answer him. [Exit.]
ISABELLA. Peace and prosperity! Who is it that calls?
[Enter LUCIO.]

LUCIO. Hail, virgin — if you are one, as those rosy cheeks announce you to be no less! Can you do me the favour of bringing me to the sight of Isabella, a novice of this house, and the fair sister of her unhappy brother Claudio?
ISABELLA. Why 'her unhappy brother'? Let me ask all the more eagerly, since I must now let you know I am that Isabella, and his sister.
LUCIO. Gentle and fair, your brother sends his kind greetings. Not to keep you in suspense — he is in prison.
ISABELLA. Alas! For what?
LUCIO. For something that, if I were his judge, would earn him thanks rather than punishment. He has got his sweetheart with child.
ISABELLA. Sir, don't make me the butt of your story.

LUCIO. It is true. I would not, though it is my common sin with girls to play the lapwing and to joke with my tongue far from my heart — play that way with all virgins. I hold you as something set above and made holy; by your renunciation, an immortal spirit; and to be spoken with sincerely, as one would speak with a saint.
ISABELLA. You blaspheme what is good by mocking me.

LUCIO. Don't believe it. In few and true words, it's this: your brother and his lover have embraced. As those that feed grow full — as the blossoming season, which from the seeding bare fallow brings teeming abundance — even so her full womb proclaims his thorough sowing and husbandry.
ISABELLA. Someone with child by him? My cousin Juliet?
LUCIO. Is she your cousin?
ISABELLA. Adoptively — as schoolgirls change their names out of fond, though apt, affection.
LUCIO. It is she.
ISABELLA. Oh, let him marry her.

LUCIO. There's the trouble. The duke has very strangely gone from here. He led many gentlemen, myself among them, to expect action; but we learn from those who know the very nerves of state that his announcements were at an infinite distance from his true intent. In his place, with the full authority of his office, Lord Angelo governs — a man whose blood is melted-snow water; one who never feels the wanton stings and motions of the senses, but who blunts and dulls his natural edge with the profits of the mind, study and fasting. He — to give a scare to use and liberty, which have long run unchecked by the harsh law, as mice run past lions — has picked out an act, under whose heavy meaning your brother's life is forfeit. He arrests him on it, and closely follows the strictness of the statute to make him an example. All hope is gone, unless you have the grace, by your fair pleading, to soften Angelo. And that's the heart of my errand between you and your poor brother.
ISABELLA. Does he so seek his life?
LUCIO. He has sentenced him already; and, as I hear, the provost already has a warrant for his execution.
ISABELLA. Alas! What little ability is in me to do him good?
LUCIO. Try the power you have.
ISABELLA. My power? Alas, I doubt—

LUCIO. Our doubts are traitors, and make us lose the good we might often win by being afraid to attempt it. Go to Lord Angelo, and let him learn to know that when maidens plead, men give like gods; but when they weep and kneel, all their petitions are as freely granted them as if the men themselves would owe them.
ISABELLA. I'll see what I can do.
LUCIO. But quickly.

ISABELLA. I'll go about it at once. I won't stay any longer than to give the Mother Superior notice of my errand. I humbly thank you. Commend me to my brother. Soon, by tonight, I'll send him certain word of how I succeed.
LUCIO. I take my leave of you.
ISABELLA. Good sir, adieu.
[Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 4.

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — _A hall in ANGELO'S house._
paragraphs: [Enter ANGELO, ESCALUS, and a Justice, Provost, Officers, and other Attendants, behind.]
ANGELO. We must not make a scarecrow of the law, setting it up to frighten the birds of prey, and letting it keep one shape until familiarity turns it into their perch rather than their terror.

ESCALUS. Yes, but still — let us be sharp, and rather cut a little than strike and bruise to death. Alas, this gentleman, whom I'd save, had a most noble father! Let your honour, whom I believe to be most strict in virtue, just consider: in the workings of your own feelings, if time had matched with opportunity, or opportunity with desire, or if the determined acting out of your blood could have reached the end of its own purpose — whether you might not, at some time in your life, have erred in the very point you now condemn him for, and brought the law upon yourself.

ANGELO. It's one thing to be tempted, Escalus, another thing to fall. I don't deny that the jury, ruling on the prisoner's life, may have among its sworn twelve a thief or two guiltier than the man they try. What is exposed to justice, justice seizes; how do the laws know that thieves pass judgment on thieves? It's plain enough — the jewel we find, we stoop and pick up because we see it; but what we don't see, we tread upon, and never think of. You may not excuse his offence on the grounds that I have had such faults; rather, tell me, when I, who condemn him, commit the same offence, let my own judgement model my death, and let nothing be made partial. Sir, he must die.
ESCALUS. Be it as your wisdom decides.
ANGELO. Where is the provost?
PROVOST. Here, if it please your honour.
ANGELO. See that Claudio is executed by nine tomorrow morning. Bring him his confessor; let him be prepared, for that's the limit of his pilgrimage. [Exit Provost.]
ESCALUS. [Aside] Well, heaven forgive him! And forgive us all! Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall; some run from thickets of ice and answer nothing; and some are condemned for one fault alone.
[Enter ELBOW, and Officers with FROTH and POMPEY.]
ELBOW. Come, bring them on. If these are decent people in a commonwealth, doing nothing but practising their abuses in common houses, then I know no law. Bring them on.
ANGELO. How now, sir! What's your name? And what's the matter?
ELBOW. If it please your honour, I am the poor Duke's constable, and my name is Elbow. I lean, sir, upon justice, and bring before your good honour two notorious benefactors.
ANGELO. Benefactors? Well — what kind of benefactors are they? Aren't they malefactors?
ELBOW. If it please your honour, I don't well know what they are. But proper villains they are, that I am sure of, and void of all the profanation in the world that good Christians ought to have.
ESCALUS. This comes out nicely; here's a wise officer.
ANGELO. Get on with it. What sort are they? Elbow is your name? Why don't you speak, Elbow?
POMPEY. He can't, sir — he's out at elbow.
ANGELO. What are you, sir?

ELBOW. Him, sir? A tap-man, sir; part bawd; one who serves a bad woman whose house, sir, was, as they say, pulled down in the suburbs; and now she runs a bath-house, which I think is a very bad house too.
ESCALUS. How do you know that?
ELBOW. My wife, sir, whom I detest before heaven and your honour—
ESCALUS. What? Your wife?
ELBOW. Yes, sir; whom, thank heaven, is an honest woman—
ESCALUS. Do you detest her for that?
ELBOW. I say, sir, I will detest myself also, as well as her, if this house is not a bawd's house — it's a pity of her life, for it is a wicked house.
ESCALUS. How do you know that, constable?
ELBOW. By Mary, sir, by means of my wife; who, if she had been carnally inclined, might have been accused there of fornication, adultery, and every uncleanness.
ESCALUS. By the woman's doing?
ELBOW. Yes, sir, by Mistress Overdone's doing. But as she spat in his face, so she defied him.
POMPEY. Sir, if it please your honour, this is not so.
ELBOW. Prove it before these knaves here, you honourable man — prove it.
ESCALUS. Do you hear how he gets his words wrong?

POMPEY. Sir, she came in greatly with child, and craving — saving your honour's reverence — for stewed prunes. Sir, we had only two in the house, which at that very distant time stood, as it were, in a fruit dish, a dish of about three-pence. Your honours have seen such dishes — they are not china dishes, but very good dishes—
ESCALUS. Get on, get on — never mind the dish, sir.

POMPEY. No, indeed, sir, not by a pin. You're right there. But to the point: as I say, this Mistress Elbow, being, as I say, with child, and being great-bellied, and craving, as I said, for prunes; and there being only two in the dish, as I said, Master Froth here, this very man, having eaten the rest, as I said, and, as I say, paying for them very honestly — for, as you know, Master Froth, I couldn't give you change for three-pence—
FROTH. No, indeed.
POMPEY. Very well. You being then, if you remember, cracking the pits of the aforementioned prunes—
FROTH. Yes, so I did indeed.
POMPEY. Why, very well. I telling you then, if you remember, that such-and-such was past cure of the thing you know of, unless they kept very good diet, as I told you—
FROTH. All this is true.
POMPEY. Why, very well, then—
ESCALUS. Come, you are a tedious fool. To the point. What was done to Elbow's wife, that he has cause to complain of? Get me to what was done to her.
POMPEY. Sir, your honour cannot come to that yet.
ESCALUS. No, sir, nor do I intend to.

POMPEY. Sir, but you shall come to it, by your honour's leave. And, I beseech you, look into Master Froth here, sir — a man of eighty pounds a year, whose father died at Hallowmas — was it not at Hallowmas, Master Froth?
FROTH. All-Hallows' Eve.
POMPEY. Why, very well. I hope here be truths. He, sir, sitting, as I say, in a lower chair, sir — it was in the Bunch of Grapes, where, indeed, you have a delight to sit, do you not?
FROTH. I do, because it is an open room, and good for winter.
POMPEY. Why, very well, then. I hope here be truths.
ANGELO. This will last out a night in Russia, where the nights are longest. I'll take my leave, and leave you to the hearing of the case; hoping you'll find good cause to whip them all.
ESCALUS. I think no less. Good morning to your lordship.
[Exit Angelo.]
Now, sir, come on. What was done to Elbow's wife, once more?
POMPEY. Once, sir? There was nothing done to her once.
ELBOW. I beseech you, sir, ask him what this man did to my wife.
POMPEY. I beseech your honour, ask me.
ESCALUS. Well, sir, what did this gentleman do to her?
POMPEY. I beseech you, sir, look at this gentleman's face. Good Master Froth, look upon his honour — it's for a good purpose. Does your honour mark his face?
ESCALUS. Yes, sir, very well.
POMPEY. No, I beseech you, mark it well.
ESCALUS. Well, I do so.
POMPEY. Does your honour see any harm in his face?
ESCALUS. Why, no.

POMPEY. I'll be sworn on a book, his face is the worst thing about him. Good, then — if his face is the worst thing about him, how could Master Froth have done the constable's wife any harm? I'd like to know that of your honour.
ESCALUS. He's in the right. Constable, what do you say to it?
ELBOW. First, if it please you, the house is a respected house; next, this is a respected fellow; and his mistress is a respected woman.
POMPEY. By this hand, sir, his wife is a more respected person than any of us.
ELBOW. Knave, you lie; you lie, wicked knave! The time is yet to come that she was ever respected with man, woman, or child.
POMPEY. Sir, she was respected with him before he married her.
ESCALUS. Which is the wiser here? Justice or Iniquity? Is this true?

ELBOW. O you caitiff! O you knave! O you wicked Hannibal! I respected with her before I was married to her? If ever I was respected with her, or she with me, let not your worship think me the poor Duke's officer. Prove this, you wicked Hannibal, or I'll bring my action of battery against you.
ESCALUS. If he gave you a box on the ear, you might bring your action of slander too.
ELBOW. By Mary, I thank your good worship for it. What is your worship's pleasure I should do with this wicked caitiff?
ESCALUS. Truly, officer, because he has some offences in him that you would discover if you could, let him continue in his ways till you know what they are.
ELBOW. By Mary, I thank your worship for it. You see, you wicked knave, now, what's come upon you — you are to continue now, you knave; you are to continue.
ESCALUS. Where were you born, friend?
FROTH. Here in Vienna, sir.
ESCALUS. Are you of eighty pounds a year?
FROTH. Yes, if it please you, sir.
ESCALUS. So. What trade are you of, sir?
POMPEY. A tap-man — a poor widow's tap-man.
ESCALUS. Your mistress' name?
POMPEY. Mistress Overdone.
ESCALUS. Has she had more than one husband?
POMPEY. Nine, sir; Overdone by the last.

ESCALUS. Nine! Come over here to me, Master Froth. Master Froth, I would not have you associating with tap-men — they will draw you in, Master Froth, and you will hang them. Get going, and let me hear no more of you.
FROTH. I thank your worship. For my own part, I never come into any room in a tap-house without being drawn in.
ESCALUS. Well, no more of it, Master Froth — farewell.
[Exit Froth.] Come over here to me, Master tap-man.
What's your name, Master tap-man?
POMPEY. Pompey.
ESCALUS. What else?
POMPEY. Bum, sir.

ESCALUS. Truly, your bum is the biggest thing about you; so that, in the coarsest sense, you are Pompey the Great. Pompey, you are partly a bawd, Pompey, however you dress it up as being a tap-man, are you not? Come, tell me true — it shall be the better for you.
POMPEY. Truly, sir, I am a poor fellow who wants to make a living.
ESCALUS. How would you make a living, Pompey? By being a bawd? What do you think of the trade, Pompey? Is it a lawful trade?
POMPEY. If the law would allow it, sir.
ESCALUS. But the law will not allow it, Pompey; nor shall it be allowed in Vienna.
POMPEY. Does your worship mean to geld and spay all the youth of the city?
ESCALUS. No, Pompey.
POMPEY. Truly, sir, in my poor opinion, they'll get to it then. If your worship will take measures for the prostitutes and the rogues, you needn't fear the bawds.
ESCALUS. There are pretty measures beginning, I can tell you — it's nothing but beheading and hanging.

POMPEY. If you behead and hang everyone who offends that way for ten years together, you'll be glad to issue a commission for more heads. If this law holds in Vienna for ten years, I'll rent the finest house in it at three-pence a section. If you live to see this come to pass, say Pompey told you so.

ESCALUS. Thank you, good Pompey; and, in return for your prophecy, listen: I advise you, let me not find you before me again on any complaint whatsoever — no, not even for dwelling where you do. If I do, Pompey, I shall beat you back to your tent, and prove a shrewd Caesar to you. In plain dealing, Pompey, I shall have you whipped. So, for this time, Pompey, farewell.
POMPEY. I thank your worship for your good counsel;
[Aside] but I shall follow it as the flesh and fortune shall
better determine.
Whip me? No, no — let the carter whip his nag. The valiant heart is not whipped out of his trade. [Exit.]
ESCALUS. Come over here to me, Master Elbow; come here, Master constable. How long have you been in this post of constable?
ELBOW. Seven years and a half, sir.
ESCALUS. I thought, by your skill in the office, you had been in it some time. You say, seven years together?
ELBOW. And a half, sir.
ESCALUS. Alas, it must have been hard on you. They do you wrong to put you to it so often. Are there no men in your ward able enough to serve?
ELBOW. Faith, sir, few of any sense in such matters. As they're chosen, they're glad to choose me instead. I do it for a bit of money, and see it all through.
ESCALUS. Bring me in the names of about six or seven, the most capable of your parish.
ELBOW. To your worship's house, sir?
ESCALUS. To my house. Farewell. [Exit Elbow.] What's the time, do you think?
JUSTICE. Eleven, sir.
ESCALUS. I pray you, home to dinner with me.
JUSTICE. I humbly thank you.
ESCALUS. It grieves me about the death of Claudio; but there's no help for it.
JUSTICE. Lord Angelo is severe.
ESCALUS. It is only what's needful. Mercy is not itself, that often looks so; pardon is still the nurse of further wrong. But yet — poor Claudio! There's no help for it. Come, sir. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: II, 1.

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — _Another room in the same._
paragraphs: [Enter PROVOST and a Servant.]
SERVANT. He's hearing a cause; he will come straight. I'll tell him about you.
PROVOST. Please do. [Exit Servant.] I'll know his pleasure; perhaps he will relent. Alas, he has only offended as in a dream! All sects, all ages have a taste of this vice; and he to die for it!
[Enter ANGELO.]
ANGELO. Now, what's the matter, provost?
PROVOST. Is it your will that Claudio shall die tomorrow?
ANGELO. Didn't I tell you yes? Didn't you have the order? Why do you ask again?
PROVOST. In case I should be too rash. Under your good correction, I have seen — when, after execution, Judgement has repented its sentence.
ANGELO. Get on; let that be my concern. Do your office, or give up your place, and you shall be well spared.
PROVOST. I beg your honour's pardon. What shall be done, sir, with the groaning Juliet? She's very near her hour.
ANGELO. Dispose of her to some more fitting place, and that with speed.
[Re-enter Servant.]
SERVANT. Here is the sister of the condemned man, desiring access to you.
ANGELO. Has he a sister?
PROVOST. Yes, my good lord — a very virtuous maid, and shortly to be one of a sisterhood, if not already.
ANGELO. Well, let her be admitted. [Exit Servant.] See that the fornicatress is removed; let her have necessary, but not lavish, means. There shall be order for it.
[Enter ISABELLA and LUCIO.]
PROVOST. God save your honour!
ANGELO. Stay a little while. [To Isabella] You're welcome. What's your will?
ISABELLA. I am a woeful suitor to your honour, if it please your honour to hear me.
ANGELO. Well, what's your suit?

ISABELLA. There is a vice that most I do abhor, and most I desire should meet the blow of justice — for which I would not plead, but that I must; for which I must not plead, but that I am at war between will and will not.
ANGELO. Well, the matter?
ISABELLA. I have a brother who is condemned to die. I do beseech you, let it be his fault, and not my brother.
PROVOST. [Aside] Heaven give you moving graces!

ANGELO. Condemn the fault, and not the actor of it? Why, every fault's condemned before it's done. Mine would be the very figure of nothing as an office, to fine the faults whose fine is already on record, and let the offender go by.
ISABELLA. O just but severe law! I had a brother, then — Heaven keep your honour!

LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] Don't give it up like that. Go to him again, plead with him. Kneel down before him, hang upon his gown. You are too cold; if you needed a pin, you couldn't ask for it with a tamer tongue. To him, I say!
ISABELLA. Must he necessarily die?
ANGELO. Maiden, there's no remedy.
ISABELLA. Yes — I do think that you might pardon him, and neither heaven nor man would grieve at the mercy.
ANGELO. I will not do it.
ISABELLA. But can you, if you would?
ANGELO. Look — what I will not, that I cannot do.
ISABELLA. But could you do it, and do the world no wrong, if your heart were touched with the same remorse for him as mine is?
ANGELO. He's sentenced; it's too late.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] You are too cold.

ISABELLA. Too late? Why, no. I, who can speak a word, can call it back again. Well, believe this: no ceremony that belongs to the great — not the king's crown, nor the deputed sword, the marshal's truncheon, nor the judge's robe — becomes them half so well as mercy does. If he had been as you, and you as he, you would have slipped like him; but he, like you, would not have been so stern.
ANGELO. Please, be gone.
ISABELLA. I wish to heaven I had your power, and you were Isabel! Should it then be like this? No — I would tell you what it is to be a judge, and what it is to be a prisoner.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] Yes, touch him; there's the vein.
ANGELO. Your brother is a forfeit of the law, and you only waste your words.

ISABELLA. Alas, alas! Why, all the souls that ever were, were forfeit once; and He that could best have taken the advantage, found out the remedy. How would you be, if He, who is at the top of judgement, were only to judge you as you are? Oh, think on that — and mercy will then breathe within your lips, like a man newly made.
ANGELO. Be content, fair maid. It is the law, not I, that condemns your brother. Were he my kinsman, brother, or my son, it would be like this with him: he must die tomorrow.

ISABELLA. Tomorrow! Oh, that's sudden! Spare him, spare him! He is not prepared for death. Even for our kitchens we kill the fowl in season; shall we serve heaven with less respect than we minister to our gross selves? Good, good my lord — think on this. Who is it that has died for this offence? Many have committed it.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] Yes, well said.

ANGELO. The law has not been dead, though it has slept. Those many would not have dared to do that evil, if the first who broke the edict had answered for his deed. Now it is awake, takes note of what is done; and, like a prophet, looks in a glass that shows what future evils — either now, or newly conceived through negligence, and so in progress to be hatched and born — are now to have no successive degrees, but, before they live, to be ended.
ISABELLA. Yet show some pity.

ANGELO. I show it most of all when I show justice. For then I pity those I do not know, whom a dismissed offence would later gall; and I do right by him who, answering for one foul wrong, lives not to commit another. Be satisfied — your brother dies tomorrow; be content.
ISABELLA. So you must be the first that gives this sentence, and he the one who suffers it. Oh, it is excellent to have a giant's strength, but it is tyrannous to use it like a giant.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] That's well said.

ISABELLA. Could great men thunder as Jove himself does, Jove would never be quiet, for every paltry, petty officer would use his heaven for thunder — nothing but thunder! Merciful Heaven, you would rather, with your sharp and sulphurous bolt, split the unwedgeable and gnarled oak than the soft myrtle; but man, proud man, dressed in a little brief authority, most ignorant of what he is most assured of — his glassy essence — like an angry ape plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven as make the angels weep, who, with our spleens, would all laugh themselves mortal.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] Oh, to him, to him, girl! He will relent; he's coming round, I can see it.
PROVOST. [Aside] Pray heaven she wins him!
ISABELLA. We cannot weigh our brother against ourselves. Great men may jest with saints; it is wit in them, but in the lesser it is foul profanation.
LUCIO. You're in the right, girl; more of that.
ISABELLA. That which in the captain is only a quick-tempered word is in the soldier flat blasphemy.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] Are you wise to that? More of it.
ANGELO. Why do you put these sayings on me?

ISABELLA. Because authority, though it errs like others, has yet a kind of medicine in itself, that skins over the vice on the surface. Go to your bosom; knock there, and ask your heart what it knows that's like my brother's fault. If it confesses a natural guiltiness such as his, let it not sound a thought upon your tongue against my brother's life.
ANGELO. [Aside] She speaks, and it is such sense, that my sense breeds with it. Fare you well.
ISABELLA. Gentle my lord, turn back.
ANGELO. I will think on it. Come again tomorrow.
ISABELLA. Listen how I'll bribe you: good my lord, turn back.
ANGELO. What? Bribe me?
ISABELLA. Yes, with such gifts that heaven shall share with you.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] You would have spoiled it all otherwise.

ISABELLA. Not with foolish shekels of the assayed gold, or stones whose rates are either rich or poor as fancy values them; but with true prayers that shall be up at heaven and enter there before sun-rise — prayers from preserved souls, from fasting maids whose minds are dedicated to nothing temporal.
ANGELO. Well — come to me tomorrow.
LUCIO. [Aside to Isabella] Get on; it's well; away!
ISABELLA. Heaven keep your honour safe!
ANGELO. [Aside] Amen — for I am that way going to temptation, where prayers cross.
ISABELLA. At what hour tomorrow shall I attend your lordship?
ANGELO. At any time before noon.
ISABELLA. God save your honour!
[Exeunt Isabella, Lucio, and Provost.]

ANGELO. From you — even from your virtue! What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine? The tempter or the tempted, who sins most? Ha! Not she; nor does she tempt — but it is I, that, lying by the violet in the sun, do as the carrion does, not as the flower, corrupting with virtuous season. Can it be that modesty may more betray our sense than woman's lightness? Having waste ground enough, shall we desire to raze the sanctuary, and pitch our evils there? O fie, fie, fie! What do you, or what are you, Angelo? Do you desire her foully for those very things that make her good? Oh, let her brother live — thieves for their robbery have authority when judges steal themselves. What, do I love her, that I desire to hear her speak again, and feast upon her eyes? What is it I dream on? O cunning enemy, that, to catch a saint, with saints you bait your hook! Most dangerous is that temptation that goads us on to sin in loving virtue. Never could the strumpet, with all her double vigour — art and nature — once stir my temper; but this virtuous maid subdues me completely. Ever until now, when men were fond, I smiled, and wondered how. [Exit.]
NOTES: II, 2.

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — _A room in a prison._
paragraphs: [Enter, severally, DUKE disguised as a friar, and PROVOST.]
DUKE. Hail to you, provost! — so I think you are.
PROVOST. I am the provost. What's your will, good friar?

DUKE. Bound by my charity and my blessed order, I come to visit the afflicted spirits here in the prison. Do me the common right to let me see them, and to make me know the nature of their crimes, so that I may minister to them accordingly.
PROVOST. I would do more than that, if more were needful.
[Enter JULIET.]

Look, here comes one — a gentlewoman of mine, who, falling in the flaws of her own youth, has blistered her reputation. She is with child; and he that got it sentenced — a young man more fit to do another such offence than die for this.
DUKE. When must he die?
PROVOST. As I think, tomorrow. I have provided for you. Stay a while, [To Juliet] and you shall be conducted.
DUKE. Do you repent, fair one, of the sin you carry?
JULIET. I do; and bear the shame most patiently.
DUKE. I'll teach you how to arraign your conscience, and try your penitence — whether it be sound, or hollowly put on.
JULIET. I'll gladly learn.
DUKE. Do you love the man that wronged you?
JULIET. Yes, as I love the woman that wronged him.
DUKE. So, then, it seems your most offensive act was mutually committed?
JULIET. Mutually.
DUKE. Then was your sin of heavier kind than his.
JULIET. I do confess it, and repent it, father.

DUKE. That is fitting, daughter — but lest you repent only because the sin has brought you to this shame, which sorrow is always towards ourselves, not heaven, showing that we would not spare heaven out of love for it, but only because we stand in fear of it —
JULIET. I do repent of it, as it is an evil, and take the shame with joy.
DUKE. Rest there. Your partner, as I hear, must die tomorrow, and I am going with instruction to him. Grace go with you, Benedicite! [Exit.]
JULIET. Must die tomorrow! O injurious love, that respites me a life whose very comfort is still a dying horror!
PROVOST. It's pity of him. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: II, 3.

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — _A room in ANGELO'S house._
paragraphs: [Enter ANGELO.]

ANGELO. When I would pray and think, I think and pray to several subjects. Heaven has my empty words, while my invention, not hearing my tongue, anchors on Isabel. Heaven is in my mouth, as if I did but only chew his name; and in my heart, the strong and swelling evil of my conception. The state, which I studied, is like a good thing, often read — grown feared and tedious; yes, my gravity, in which — let no man hear me — I take pride, I could with profit change for an idle plume that the air beats for nothing. O place, O form, how often do you, with your case and your habit, wrench awe out of fools, and tie the wiser souls to your false seeming! Blood, you are blood — let's write 'good angel' on the devil's horn; it is not the devil's crest.
[Enter a Servant.]
How now! Who's there?
SERVANT. One Isabel, a sister, desires access to you.

ANGELO. Show her the way. O heavens! Why does my blood thus muster to my heart, making it both unable for itself, and dispossessing all my other parts of necessary fitness? So play the foolish throngs with one that swoons — come all to help him, and so stop up the air by which he should revive. And even so the general, subject to a well-wished king, quit their own part, and in obsequious fondness crowd to his presence, where their untaught love must needs appear an offence.
[Enter ISABELLA.]
How now, fair maid?
ISABELLA. I am come to know your pleasure.
ANGELO. That you might know it would much better please me than to have you demand what it is. Your brother cannot live.
ISABELLA. Even so. — Heaven keep your honour!
ANGELO. Yet he may live a while; and, it may be, as long as you or I. Yet he must die.
ISABELLA. Under your sentence?
ANGELO. Yes. ISABELLA. When, I beseech you? — so that in his reprieve, longer or shorter, he may be so prepared that his soul does not sicken.

ANGELO. Ha! Fie, these filthy vices! It were as good to pardon him that has from nature stolen a man already made, as to remit their saucy sweetness that do coin heaven's image in stamps that are forbid. It is all as easy falsely to take away a life truly made, as to put metal in restrained means to make a false one.
ISABELLA. It is set down so in heaven, but not on earth.

ANGELO. Say you so? Then I shall pose you quickly. Which would you rather — that the most just law should now take your brother's life; or, to redeem him, give up your body to such sweet uncleanness as she that he has stained?
ISABELLA. Sir, believe this: I had rather give my body than my soul.
ANGELO. I'm not talking of your soul. Our compelled sins stand more for number than for account.
ISABELLA. What do you say?

ANGELO. No, I won't warrant that; for I can speak against the thing I say. Answer to this: I, now the voice of the recorded law, pronounce a sentence on your brother's life. Might there not be a charity in sin to save this brother's life?
ISABELLA. If it please you to do it, I will take it as a peril to my soul, it is no sin at all, but charity.
ANGELO. If you were pleased to do it at peril of your soul, it would be an equal poise of sin and charity.

ISABELLA. That I do beg his life — if it be sin, heaven let me bear it! Your granting of my suit, if that be sin, I'll make it my morning prayer to have added to the faults of mine, and nothing of your answer.
ANGELO. No, but hear me. Your sense does not pursue mine. Either you are ignorant, or you seem so, craftily; and that is not good.
ISABELLA. Let me be ignorant, and in nothing good, but graciously to know I am no better.

ANGELO. Thus wisdom wishes to appear most bright when it taxes itself; as these black masks proclaim a hidden beauty ten times louder than beauty could, displayed. But mark me: to be received plainly, I'll speak more bluntly. Your brother is to die.
ISABELLA. So.
ANGELO. And his offence is such, as it appears, accountable to the law for that penalty.
ISABELLA. True.

ANGELO. Admit there were no other way to save his life — as I do not subscribe to that, nor to any other, but only in the loss of argument — that you, his sister, finding yourself desired by such a person, whose credit with the judge, or own great place, could fetch your brother from the manacles of the all-building law; and that there were no earthly means to save him, but that you must either lay down the treasures of your body to this supposed person, or else let him suffer — what would you do?

ISABELLA. As much for my poor brother as for myself. That is — were I under sentence of death, I would wear the impression of keen whips as rubies, and strip myself to death as to a bed that I had been sick with longing for, before I would yield my body up to shame.
ANGELO. Then must your brother die.
ISABELLA. And it would be the cheaper way. Better it were a brother died at once, than that a sister, by redeeming him, should die for ever.
ANGELO. Were not you, then, as cruel as the sentence that you have slandered so?
ISABELLA. Ignominy in ransom, and free pardon, are of two houses; lawful mercy is in no way kin to foul redemption.
ANGELO. You seemed of late to make the law a tyrant, and rather proved the sliding of your brother a merriment than a vice.
ISABELLA. Oh, pardon me, my lord. It often falls out that, to have what we would have, we speak not what we mean. I do somewhat excuse the thing I hate, for the advantage of him I dearly love.
ANGELO. We are all frail.
ISABELLA. Else let my brother die, if not as a vassal of frailty, but only he, owe and succeed your weakness.
ANGELO. No, women are frail too.

ISABELLA. Yes, as the glasses where they view themselves — which are as easily broken as they make forms. Women! — help, Heaven! Men mar their own creation in profiting by them. No, call us ten times frail; for we are soft as our complexions are, and credulous to false prints.

ANGELO. I think it well. And, from this testimony of your own sex — since, I suppose, we are made to be no stronger than faults may shake our frames — let me be bold; I do arrest your words. Be what you are: that is, a woman. If you be more, you're none; if you be one — as you are well expressed by all external warrants — show it now, by putting on the destined livery.
ISABELLA. I have no tongue but one. Gentle my lord, let me entreat you to speak the former language.
ANGELO. Plainly understand, I love you.
ISABELLA. My brother did love Juliet, and you tell me that he shall die for it.
ANGELO. He shall not, Isabel, if you give me love.
ISABELLA. I know your virtue has a licence in it, which seems a little fouler than it is, to pluck on others.
ANGELO. Believe me, on my honour, my words express my purpose.

ISABELLA. Ha! Little honour, to be much believed! And most pernicious purpose! — Seeming, seeming! — I will proclaim you, Angelo; look for it. Sign me a present pardon for my brother, or with an outstretched throat I'll tell the world aloud what man you are.

ANGELO. Who will believe you, Isabel? My unsoiled name, the austereness of my life, my vouch against you, and my place in the state, will so outweigh your accusation, that you shall stifle in your own report, and smell of calumny. I have begun; and now I give my sensual race the rein. Fit your consent to my sharp appetite; lay by all nicety and prolixious blushes, that banish what they sue for; redeem your brother by yielding up your body to my will; or else he must not only die the death, but your unkindness shall draw out his death to lingering sufferance. Answer me tomorrow. Or, by the affection that now guides me most, I'll prove a tyrant to him. As for you, say what you can, my false will outweigh your true. [Exit.]

ISABELLA. To whom should I complain? If I told this, who would believe me? O perilous mouths, that bear in them one and the self-same tongue, either of condemnation or approval; bidding the law make courtesy to their will; hooking both right and wrong to the appetite, to follow as it draws! I'll go to my brother. Though he has fallen by the promptings of blood, yet has he in him such a mind of honour, that, had he twenty heads to tender down on twenty bloody blocks, he would yield them up, before his sister should stoop her body to such abhorred pollution. Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die: more than our brother is our chastity. I'll yet tell him of Angelo's request, and fit his mind to death, for his soul's rest. [Exit.]
NOTES: II, 4.

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — _A room in the prison._
paragraphs: [Enter DUKE disguised as before, CLAUDIO, and PROVOST.]
DUKE. So, then, you hope for pardon from Lord Angelo?
CLAUDIO. The miserable have no other medicine but only hope. I've hope to live, and am prepared to die.

DUKE. Be absolute for death; either death or life shall be the sweeter for it. Reason with life like this: if I lose you, I lose a thing that none but fools would keep. A breath you are, servile to all the influences of the sky, that hourly afflict this dwelling where you reside. To put it plainly, you are death's fool, for you labour by your flight to shun him, and yet you run toward him still. You are not noble; for all the accommodations that you carry are nursed by baseness. You are by no means valiant; for you do fear the soft and tender fork of a poor worm. Your best of rest is sleep, and that you often provoke; yet grossly you fear your death, which is no more. You are not yourself; for you exist on many a thousand grains that issue out of dust. Happy you are not; for what you do not have, you still strive to get, and what you have, you forget. You are not certain; for your complexion shifts to strange effects after the moon. If you are rich, you are poor; for, like an ass whose back is bowed with ingots, you bear your heavy riches but a journey, and death unloads you. Friend have you none; for your own bowels, which call you father, the mere effusion of your own loins, do curse the gout, serpigo, and the rheum, for not ending you sooner. You have neither youth nor age, but, as it were, an after-dinner's sleep, dreaming on both — for all your blessed youth becomes as if aged, and begs the alms of palsied old age; and when you are old and rich, you have neither heat, affection, limb, nor beauty to make your riches pleasant. What's there in this that bears the name of life? Yet in this life lie hid a thousand more deaths. And yet death we fear, which makes these odds all even.
CLAUDIO. I humbly thank you. To sue to live, I find I seek to die; and, seeking death, find life. Let it come on.
ISABELLA. [Within] What, ho! Peace here; grace and good company!
PROVOST. Who's there? Come in. The wish deserves a welcome.
DUKE. Dear sir, before long I'll visit you again.
CLAUDIO. Most holy sir, I thank you.
[Enter ISABELLA.]
ISABELLA. My business is a word or two with Claudio.
PROVOST. And very welcome. Look, signior, here's your sister.
DUKE. Provost, a word with you.
PROVOST. As many as you please.
DUKE. Bring me to hear them speak, where I may be concealed. [Exeunt Duke and Provost.]
CLAUDIO. Now, sister, what's the comfort?

ISABELLA. Why, as all comforts are: most good, most good indeed. Lord Angelo, having affairs in heaven, intends you for his swift ambassador, where you shall be an everlasting resident. Therefore make your best preparation with speed — tomorrow you set out.
CLAUDIO. Is there no remedy?
ISABELLA. None, but such a remedy as, to save a head, would cleave a heart in two.
CLAUDIO. But is there any?
ISABELLA. Yes, brother, you may live. There is a devilish mercy in the judge, that, if you'll implore it, will free your life, but fetter you till death.
CLAUDIO. Perpetual imprisonment?
ISABELLA. Yes, just so — perpetual imprisonment, a restraint, though you had all the world's vastness, to a determined scope.
CLAUDIO. But in what manner?
ISABELLA. In such a one as, if you consented to it, would strip your honour from that body you bear, and leave you naked.
CLAUDIO. Let me know the point.

ISABELLA. Oh, I fear for you, Claudio; and I tremble, lest you should embrace a feverous life, and respect six or seven winters more than a perpetual honour. Dare you die? The sense of death is most in apprehension; and the poor beetle that we tread upon, in bodily suffering finds a pang as great as when a giant dies.
CLAUDIO. Why do you give me this shame? Do you think I can fetch a resolution from flowery tenderness? If I must die, I will encounter darkness as a bride, and hug it in my arms.

ISABELLA. There spoke my brother; there my father's grave uttered forth a voice. Yes, you must die. You are too noble to preserve a life by base means. This outward-sainted deputy, whose settled face and deliberate word nips youth in the head, and pens up follies as a falcon does the fowl, is yet a devil; his filth within being cast forth, he would appear a pond as deep as hell.
CLAUDIO. The princely Angelo!
ISABELLA. Oh, it is the cunning livery of hell, to invest and cover the most damnable body in princely guise! Do you think, Claudio? — if I would yield him my virginity, you might be freed.
CLAUDIO. O heavens! It cannot be.
ISABELLA. Yes, he would give it you, from this rank offence, so that you might offend him still. This night is the time that I should do what I abhor to name, or else you die tomorrow.
CLAUDIO. You shall not do it.
ISABELLA. Oh, were it but my life, I'd throw it down for your deliverance as freely as a pin.
CLAUDIO. Thanks, dear Isabel.
ISABELLA. Be ready, Claudio, for your death tomorrow.
CLAUDIO. Yes. Has he such affections in him, that he can thus make him bite the law by the nose, when he would enforce it? Surely, it is no sin; or, of the deadly seven, it is the least.
ISABELLA. Which is the least?
CLAUDIO. If it were damnable, he being so wise, why would he, for the momentary trick, be everlastingly fined? Oh Isabel!
ISABELLA. What says my brother?
CLAUDIO. Death is a fearful thing.
ISABELLA. And a shamed life a hateful one.

CLAUDIO. Yes, but to die, and go we know not where; to lie in cold obstruction and to rot; this sensible warm motion to become a kneaded clod; and the delighted spirit to bathe in fiery floods, or to reside in thrilling region of thick-ribbed ice; to be imprisoned in the viewless winds, and blown with restless violence round about the pendent world; or to be worse than worst of those that lawless and uncertain thought imagines howling — it is too horrible! The weariest and most loathed worldly life that age, ache, penury, and imprisonment can lay on nature is a paradise to what we fear of death.
ISABELLA. Alas, alas!
CLAUDIO. Sweet sister, let me live. What sin you do to save a brother's life, nature so dispenses with the deed that it becomes a virtue.

ISABELLA. O you beast! O faithless coward! O dishonest wretch! Will you be made a man out of my vice? Is it not a kind of incest, to take life from your own sister's shame? What should I think? Heaven shield that my mother played my father fair! For such a warped slip of wildness never issued from his blood. Take my defiance! Die, perish! If only my kneeling down could reprieve you from your fate, it should proceed. I'll pray a thousand prayers for your death, no word to save you.
CLAUDIO. No, hear me, Isabel.
ISABELLA. Oh, fie, fie, fie! Your sin's not accidental, but a trade. Mercy to you would prove itself a bawd: it's best you die quickly.
CLAUDIO. Oh, hear me, Isabella!
[Re-enter DUKE.]
DUKE. Vouchsafe a word, young sister, but one word.
ISABELLA. What is your will?
DUKE. If you might spare some of your time, I would by and by have some speech with you. The satisfaction I would require is likewise your own benefit.
ISABELLA. I have no superfluous leisure; my stay must be stolen out of other affairs; but I will attend on you a while.
[Walks apart.]

DUKE. Son, I have overheard what has passed between you and your sister. Angelo never had any intention to corrupt her; only he has made an assay of her virtue to practise his judgement against the disposition of natures. She, having the truth of honour in her, has made him that gracious denial which he is most glad to receive. I am confessor to Angelo, and I know this to be true. Therefore prepare yourself for death. Do not satisfy your resolution with hopes that are fallible. Tomorrow you must die. Go to your knees, and make ready.
CLAUDIO. Let me ask my sister pardon. I am so out of love with life, that I will sue to be rid of it.
DUKE. Hold yourself there. Farewell. [Exit Claudio.] Provost, a word with you!
[Re-enter PROVOST.]
PROVOST. What's your will, father?
DUKE. That, now you are come, you will be gone. Leave me a while with the maid. My mind promises with my habit that no loss shall touch her by my company.
PROVOST. In good time. [Exit Provost. Isabella comes forward.]

DUKE. The hand that has made you fair has made you good. The goodness that is cheap in beauty makes beauty brief in goodness; but grace, being the soul of your complexion, shall keep the body of it ever fair. The assault that Angelo has made upon you, fortune has conveyed to my understanding; and, but that frailty has examples for his falling, I should wonder at Angelo. How will you proceed, to satisfy this substitute, and to save your brother?

ISABELLA. I am now going to give him my answer. I had rather my brother die by the law than my son should be unlawfully born. But, oh, how much is the good Duke deceived in Angelo! If ever he return and I can speak to him, I will open my lips in vain, or expose his government.

DUKE. That shall not be much amiss; yet, as the matter now stands, he will avoid your accusation — he made trial of you only. Therefore fasten your ear on my advice: to the love I have of doing good, a remedy presents itself. I make myself believe that you may most uprightly do a poor wronged lady a deserved benefit; redeem your brother from the angry law; do no stain to your own gracious person; and much please the absent Duke, if perchance he shall ever return to have hearing of this business.
ISABELLA. Let me hear you speak further. I have spirit to do anything that is not foul to the truth of my spirit.
DUKE. Virtue is bold, and goodness never fearful. Have you not heard speak of Mariana, the sister of Frederick the great soldier who was lost at sea?
ISABELLA. I have heard of the lady, and good words went with her name.

DUKE. She was to have married this Angelo; was promised to him by oath, and the wedding appointed. Between the time of the contract and the date of the solemnity, her brother Frederick was wrecked at sea, having in that perished vessel the dowry of his sister. But mark how heavily this fell upon the poor gentlewoman: there she lost a noble and renowned brother, in his love toward her ever most kind and natural; with him, the portion and sinew of her fortune, her marriage-dowry; with both, her betrothed husband, this well-seeming Angelo.
ISABELLA. Can this be so? Did Angelo so leave her?

DUKE. Left her in her tears, and dried not one of them with his comfort; swallowed his vows whole, pretending discoveries of dishonour in her. In short, he bestowed her on her own lamentation, which she still wears for his sake; and he, a marble to her tears, is washed with them, but does not relent.
ISABELLA. What a merit it would be in death, to take this poor maid from the world! What corruption in this life, that it will let this man live! But how can she profit from this?
DUKE. It is a rupture that you may easily heal; and the cure of it not only saves your brother, but keeps you from dishonour in doing it.
ISABELLA. Show me how, good father.

DUKE. This same maid still has in her the continuance of her first affection. His unjust unkindness, that in all reason should have quenched her love, has, like an impediment in the current, made it more violent and unruly. Go to Angelo; answer his demand with a plausible obedience; agree with his demands to the point; only reserve to yourself this advantage: first, that your stay with him may not be long; that the time may have all shadow and silence in it; and the place answer to convenience. This being granted in course — and now follows the whole plan — we shall advise this wronged maid to take your place, and go in your stead. If the encounter is acknowledged hereafter, it may compel him to make amends with her. And here, by this, is your brother saved, your honour untainted, the poor Mariana advantaged, and the corrupt Deputy exposed. The maid I will prepare and make fit for his attempt. If you think well to carry this off as you may, the doubleness of the benefit defends the deceit from reproof. What think you of it?
ISABELLA. The image of it gives me content already; and I trust it will grow to a most prosperous perfection.

DUKE. It lies much in your holding up. Haste you speedily to Angelo. If for this night he entreat you to his bed, give him promise of satisfaction. I will at once go to Saint Luke's; there, at the moated grange, resides this dejected Mariana. At that place call upon me; and dispatch with Angelo, that it may be quickly done.
ISABELLA. I thank you for this comfort. Fare you well, good father.
[Exeunt severally.]
NOTES: III, 1.

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — _The street before the prison._
paragraphs: [Enter, on one side, DUKE disguised as before; on the other, ELBOW, and Officers with POMPEY.]
ELBOW. No, if there's no remedy for it, but that you will needs buy and sell men and women like beasts, we shall have all the world drink brown and white bastard.
DUKE. O heavens! What stuff is here?

POMPEY. It was never a merry world since, of two usuries, the merrier was put down, and the worse one allowed by order of law a furred gown to keep it warm — and furred with fox and lamb-skins too, to signify that craft, being richer than innocence, stands for the facing.
ELBOW. Come along, sir. God bless you, good father friar.
DUKE. And you, good brother father. What offence has this man committed against you, sir?
ELBOW. By Mary, sir, he has offended the law; and, sir, we take him to be a thief too, sir; for we have found on him, sir, a strange picklock, which we have sent to the Deputy.

DUKE. Fie, sirrah! A bawd, a wicked bawd! The evil that you cause to be done, that is your means to live. Do but think what it is to cram a stomach or clothe a back from such a filthy vice. Say to yourself: from their abominable and beastly touches I drink, I eat, dress myself, and live. Can you believe your living is a life, so stinkingly dependent? Go mend, go mend.
POMPEY. Indeed, it does stink in some sort, sir; but yet, sir, I would prove —
DUKE. No, if the devil has given you proofs for sin, you'll prove his. Take him to prison, officer. Correction and instruction must both work, before this rude beast will profit.
ELBOW. He must go before the Deputy, sir; he has given him warning. The Deputy cannot abide a whoremaster. If he be a whoremonger, and comes before him, he might as well go a mile out of his way.
DUKE. That we were all, as some would seem to be, from our faults, as faults from seeming, free!
ELBOW. His neck will come to your waist — a cord, sir.
POMPEY. I spy comfort; I cry bail. Here's a gentleman and a friend of mine.
[Enter LUCIO.]

LUCIO. How now, noble Pompey! What, at the wheels of Caesar? Are you led in triumph? What, is there none of Pygmalion's images, newly made woman, to be had now, for putting the hand in the pocket and extracting it clutched? What reply, ha? What say you to this tune, matter and method? Isn't it drowned in the last rain, ha? What say you, Trot? Is the world as it was, man? Which is the way? Is it sad, and few words — or how? What's the trick of it?
DUKE. Still thus, and thus — still worse!
LUCIO. How does my dear morsel, your mistress? Does she still procure, ha?
POMPEY. Faith, sir, she has eaten up all her beef, and she is herself in the tub.
LUCIO. Why, it's good; that's the right of it; it must be so. Always your fresh whore and your powdered bawd — an unavoidable consequence; it must be so. Are you going to prison, Pompey?
POMPEY. Yes, faith, sir.
LUCIO. Why, it's not amiss, Pompey. Farewell; go, say I sent you there. For debt, Pompey? Or how?
ELBOW. For being a bawd, for being a bawd.

LUCIO. Well, then, imprison him. If imprisonment is the due of a bawd, why, it is his right. A bawd he doubtless is, and of antiquity too — bawd-born. Farewell, good Pompey. Commend me to the prison, Pompey: you will turn good husband now, Pompey; you will keep the house.
POMPEY. I hope, sir, your good worship will be my bail.

LUCIO. No, indeed, will I not, Pompey. It is not the fashion. I will pray, Pompey, to increase your bondage. If you don't take it patiently, why, your mettle is the more. Adieu, trusty Pompey. God bless you, friar.
DUKE. And you.
LUCIO. Does Bridget paint still, Pompey, ha?
ELBOW. Come along, sir; come.
POMPEY. You will not bail me, then, sir?
LUCIO. Then nor now, Pompey. What news abroad, friar? What news?
ELBOW. Come along, sir; come.
LUCIO. Go to kennel, Pompey; go. [Exeunt Elbow, Pompey and Officers.] What news, friar, of the Duke?
DUKE. I know none. Can you tell me of any?
LUCIO. Some say he is with the Emperor of Russia; others, he is in Rome. But where is he, do you think?
DUKE. I don't know where; but wherever, I wish him well.
LUCIO. It was a mad, fantastical trick of him to steal away from the state, and usurp the beggary he was never born to. Lord Angelo plays the duke well in his absence; he puts transgression to it.
DUKE. He does well in it.
LUCIO. A little more leniency to lechery would do no harm in him; he's something too crabbed that way, friar.
DUKE. It is too general a vice, and severity must cure it.

LUCIO. Yes, in good truth, the vice is of a great kindred; it is well allied. But it is impossible to extirpate it quite, friar, till eating and drinking be put down. They say this Angelo was not made by man and woman after this downright way of creation. Is it true, do you think?
DUKE. How should he be made, then?

LUCIO. Some say a sea-maid spawned him; some, that he was begot between two stock-fishes. But it is certain that, when he makes water, his urine is congealed ice; that I know to be true. And he is a motion generative; that's infallible.
DUKE. You are pleasant, sir, and speak rapidly.

LUCIO. Why, what a ruthless thing is this in him, for the rebellion of a codpiece to take away the life of a man! Would the Duke that is absent have done this? Before he would have hanged a man for the getting of a hundred bastards, he would have paid for the nursing of a thousand. He had some feeling of the sport; he knew the service, and that instructed him to mercy.
DUKE. I never heard the absent Duke much suspected for women; he was not inclined that way.
LUCIO. Oh, sir, you are deceived.
DUKE. It is not possible.
LUCIO. Who, not the Duke? Yes — your beggar of fifty; and his custom was to put a ducat in her clack-dish. The Duke had crotchets in him. He would be drunk too; let me inform you of that.
DUKE. You do him wrong, surely.
LUCIO. Sir, I was an intimate of his. A shy fellow was the Duke; and I believe I know the cause of his withdrawing.
DUKE. What, I pray you, might be the cause?
LUCIO. No, pardon — it is a secret must be locked within the teeth and the lips. But this I can let you understand: the greater number of his subjects held the Duke to be wise.
DUKE. Wise! Why, no question but he was.
LUCIO. A very superficial, ignorant, unweighing fellow.

DUKE. Either this is envy in you, folly, or mistaking. The very stream of his life, and the business he has helmed, must, upon a warranted need, give him a better proclamation. Let him only be testified to in his own actions, and he shall appear, to the envious, a scholar, a statesman, and a soldier. Therefore you speak unskilfully; or, if your knowledge be more, it is much darkened in your malice.
LUCIO. Sir, I know him, and I love him.
DUKE. Love talks with better knowledge, and knowledge with dearer love.
LUCIO. Come, sir, I know what I know.

DUKE. I can hardly believe that, since you know not what you speak. But, if ever the Duke returns, as our prayers are he may, let me desire you to make your answer before him. If what you have spoken is honest, you have courage to maintain it. I am bound to call upon you; and, I pray you, your name?
LUCIO. Sir, my name is Lucio; well known to the duke.
DUKE. He shall know you better, sir, if I live to report you.
LUCIO. I do not fear you.
DUKE. Oh, you hope the Duke will return no more; or you imagine me too harmless an opposite. But, indeed, I can do you little harm; you'll forswear this again.
LUCIO. I'll be hanged first. You are deceived in me, friar. But no more of this. Can you tell if Claudio dies tomorrow or no?
DUKE. Why should he die, sir?

LUCIO. Why? For filling a bottle with a tun-dish. I wish the Duke we talk of were returned again. This ungenitured agent will unpeople the province with continency; sparrows must not build in his house-eaves, because they are lecherous. The Duke would yet have had dark deeds darkly answered; he would never have brought them to light. Would he were returned! By Mary, this Claudio is condemned for untrussing. Farewell, good friar; I pray you, pray for me. The Duke, I say to you again, would eat mutton on Fridays. He's not past it yet; and I say to you, he would mouth with a beggar, though she smelt of brown bread and garlic. Say that I said so. Farewell. [Exit.]
DUKE. No might nor greatness in mortality can escape censure; back-wounding calumny strikes the whitest virtue. What king so strong can tie up the gall in the slanderous tongue? But who comes here?
[Enter ESCALUS, PROVOST, and Officers with MISTRESS OVERDONE.]
ESCALUS. Go; away with her to prison!
MISTRESS OVERDONE. Good my lord, be good to me; your honour is reckoned a merciful man; good my lord.
ESCALUS. Double and treble admonition, and still forfeit in the same kind! This would make mercy itself swear and play the tyrant.
PROVOST. A bawd of eleven years' continuance, may it please your honour.

MISTRESS OVERDONE. My lord, this is one Lucio's information against me. Mistress Kate Keepdown was with child by him in the Duke's time; he promised her marriage. His child is a year and a quarter old, come Philip and Jacob — I have kept it myself; and see how he goes about to abuse me!

ESCALUS. That fellow is a fellow of much licence. Let him be called before us. Away with her to prison! Get on; no more words. [Exeunt Officers with Mistress Overdone.] Provost, my brother Angelo will not be altered; Claudio must die tomorrow. Let him be furnished with divines, and have all charitable preparation. If my brother were to act by my pity, it should not be so with him.
PROVOST. So please you, this friar has been with him, and advised him for the receiving of death.
ESCALUS. Good evening, good father.
DUKE. Bliss and goodness on you!
ESCALUS. Where are you from?
DUKE. Not of this country, though my chance now is to use it for my time. I am a brother of a gracious order, lately come from the See on special business from his Holiness.
ESCALUS. What news abroad in the world?

DUKE. None, but that there is so great a fever on goodness, that the dissolution of it must cure it. Novelty is only in request; and it is as dangerous to be aged in any kind of course, as it is virtuous to be constant in any undertaking. There is scarcely truth enough alive to make societies secure; but security enough to make fellowships accursed — much upon this riddle runs the wisdom of the world. This news is old enough, yet it is every day's news. I pray you, sir, of what disposition was the Duke?
ESCALUS. One that, above all other strifes, contended especially to know himself.
DUKE. What pleasure was he given to?

ESCALUS. Rather rejoicing to see another merry, than merry at anything that professed to make him rejoice — a gentleman of all temperance. But leave we him to his events, with a prayer they may prove prosperous; and let me desire to know how you find Claudio prepared. I am given to understand that you have lent him visitation.

DUKE. He professes to have received no sinister measure from his judge, but most willingly humbles himself to the determination of justice. Yet had he framed to himself, by the instruction of his frailty, many deceiving promises of life; which I, in my good leisure, have discredited to him, and now he is resolved to die.

ESCALUS. You have paid the heavens your function, and the prisoner the very debt of your calling. I have laboured for the poor gentleman to the extremest shore of my modesty; but my brother justice have I found so severe, that he has forced me to tell him he is indeed Justice.
DUKE. If his own life answers the strictness of his proceeding, it shall become him well; wherein, if he chance to fail, he has sentenced himself.
ESCALUS. I am going to visit the prisoner. Fare you well.
DUKE. Peace be with you! [Exeunt Escalus and Provost.]

He who the sword of heaven will bear should be as holy as severe; pattern in himself to know, grace to stand, and virtue go; paying no more nor less to others than by self-offences weighing. Shame to him whose cruel striking kills for faults of his own liking! Twice treble shame on Angelo, to weed my vice and let his grow! Oh, what may man hide within him, though angel on the outward side! How may likeness made in crimes, making practice on the times, draw with idle spiders' strings most ponderous and substantial things! Craft against vice I must apply: with Angelo tonight shall lie his old betrothed, but despised; so disguise shall, by the disguised, pay with falsehood false exacting, and perform an old contracting. [Exit.]
NOTES: III, 2.
